newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Sydney Olympic rings become eggs in protest.
newsitem.headline: Sydney Olympic rings become eggs in protest.

text.p: Sydney Olympic 2000 organisers have issued the first writ over alleged misuse of the official Games logo, against an animal rights activist who turned the Olympic rings into chicken eggs.
Pam Clarke, who campaigns against "battery hens", has been served a writ to stop using the modified Games logo on T-shirts with the slogan Freedom 2000, Olympic organisers said on Friday.
Battery hens is a term used for the mass production of eggs using rows of chickens in cages.
"Basically she has used the whole logo, but turned the rings into eggs." said spokeswoman Tracey Holmes of the Sydney Organising Committee of the Olympic Games (SOCOG).
An unrepentant Clarke defended the altered artwork, saying the logo, which depicts a stylised runner trailing a streamer, also looked like a "sad hen" when viewed from right to left.
"Once you see the bird, you can't go back to the runner," Clarke told Reuters in a telephone interview from her home in the island state of Tasmania.
"It's a gift. I didn't have to make any changes."
Clarke said she had simply altered the Olympic rings to eggs and printed 500 T-shirts, selling a few hundred for a profit of about A$500 (US$380) for her campaign.
A 15-year veteran of animal rights campaigns, Clarke said she had spent 80 days in jail for protests against caged hens and was delighted with the publicity from her latest idea.
"I want to string it out if I can...we've got three years to go on this," Clarke said.
SOCOG's Holmes said Games organisers had a duty to protect the logo and its value for official sponsors.
Unauthorised use of Olympic logos was a problem at every Games, but Sydney organisers had seen no other cases so far.
"I think the word got out fairly early on with Sydney 2000 that it wouldn't be tolerated," Holmes said.
